p.src: Could Space Repeat Before the Horizon?

u.src: Could Space Repeat Before the Horizon?
en: Could Space Repeat Before the Horizon?

p.src: A finite flat universe can be represented by a periodic cell. If that cell were smaller than the observable region, light could traverse it and the sky would contain repeated views of the same structures. Detecting those repetitions is harder than simply recognizing a familiar galaxy: the images arrive from different directions and epochs and are altered by cosmic evolution. Nevertheless, periodic topology has observable consequences.

p.src: Expansion Does Not Pull Apart Bound Systems

u.src: Expansion Does Not Pull Apart Bound Systems
en: Expansion Does Not Pull Apart Bound Systems

p.src: Cosmic expansion describes the large-scale motion of freely moving matter in the average cosmological geometry. It is not a universal command that every proper length must increase. Electromagnetic forces bind atoms, gravity binds planetary systems, and ordinary molecular forces bind solid objects. These interactions are enormously stronger than the cosmological correction on such scales.

p.src: The remaining objection is not about force but bookkeeping. If a bound orbit continually resists a small cosmological perturbation, where does the required energy come from? The premise imports a conservation law from a static background into a spacetime that has no global time-translation symmetry.

p.src: Homogeneity Is a Coarse-Grained Statement

u.src: Homogeneity Is a Coarse-Grained Statement
en: Homogeneity Is a Coarse-Grained Statement

p.src: The cosmological principle is scale dependent. Air in a closed room may be nearly uniform on the scale of the room but is granular on molecular scales. The universe likewise contains planets, galaxies, clusters, and density fluctuations. Homogeneity and isotropy refer to its averaged behavior over distances large enough that those structures cease to select a location or direction.

p.src: Homogeneity and Isotropy as Metric Statements

u.src: Homogeneity and Isotropy as Metric Statements
en: Homogeneity and Isotropy as Metric Statements

p.src: Homogeneity and isotropy are geometrical statements before they become dynamical ones. Einstein’s equation will tell us how geometry changes with time. First we must say what kind of spatial geometry is allowed at any one time.

p.src: A space is homogeneous if an isometry can carry any point into any other point. It is isotropic about a point if rotations through that point leave its geometry unchanged. A space that is homogeneous and isotropic has neither a preferred position nor a preferred direction.

p.src:
The Euclidean plane makes the definition transparent. In Cartesian coordinates, $ds^2=dx_1^2+dx_2^2.$ Move the origin by constants $a_1$ and $a_2$: $y_1=x_1+a_1,
\qquad
y_2=x_2+a_2.$ Because $dy_i=dx_i$, the translated metric is $ds^2=dy_1^2+dy_2^2.$ The symbols used to label the point have changed, but the distance rule has not. This is the simplest realization of homogeneity. Rotations likewise preserve the metric, so the plane is isotropic as well.

p.src: The sphere is less trivial only because its coordinates are less convenient. With the south pole chosen as origin, the unit two-sphere can be written $d\Omega_2^2=dr^2+\sin^2 r\,d\theta^2.$ Rotate the sphere so that an east pole becomes the new origin. The coordinate transformation is cumbersome, but the result is again equation . No point on a round sphere is geometrically distinguished.

p.src: Intrinsic Geometry and Embedding

u.src: Intrinsic Geometry and Embedding
en: Intrinsic Geometry and Embedding

p.src: When space is called spherical, it is tempting to imagine the rubber surface of a balloon placed inside a larger room. That picture may help us draw, but the surrounding room is not part of the cosmological assertion. The geometry that matters is intrinsic: it consists of distances and angles measurable by observers who remain within the space.

p.src: Closed One-Dimensional Worlds

u.src: Closed One-Dimensional Worlds
en: Closed One-Dimensional Worlds

p.src: Consider a closed one-dimensional world. We may draw it as a circle, a square with rounded corners, or a peanut-shaped loop. An inhabitant confined to the line measures only distance along it. If two loops have the same total circumference, then those inhabitants encounter the same intrinsic geometry even when the drawings look entirely different.

p.src: Every one-dimensional metric is locally flat. A short piece of string can be straightened without stretching it, so visible bending in the surrounding plane is extrinsic rather than intrinsic curvature. A closed loop has a global modulus, its circumference, but it has no intrinsic local bending that its one-dimensional inhabitants can measure.

p.src: Why Embeddings Are Useful but Optional

u.src: Why Embeddings Are Useful but Optional
en: Why Embeddings Are Useful but Optional

p.src: We visualize a one-dimensional circle by placing it in two dimensions and a two-dimensional sphere by placing it in three. The pattern tempts us to demand a fourth Euclidean dimension before discussing a three-sphere. That demand reflects human visualization, not a mathematical necessity. Our visual machinery evolved to navigate three dimensions; coordinates and metrics let us reason beyond that limit without constructing a literal external viewpoint.

p.src: The thought experiment can be made operational. A creature restricted to the fiber could launch a signal, such as a sufficiently energetic photon, and discover an external direction only if the signal escaped the fiber and later returned by a route unavailable within the one-dimensional metric. In the same spirit, the statement that ordinary space has three large dimensions is ultimately experimental, not a deduction from what the human mind can picture.

p.src: The FRW Ansatz and the Three Curvature Cases

u.src: The FRW Ansatz and the Three Curvature Cases
en: The FRW Ansatz and the Three Curvature Cases

p.src:
The symmetry assumptions collapse the geometry to one time-dependent scale and one discrete curvature sign. In comoving coordinates the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker ansatz is $ds^2=-dt^2+a(t)^2\,d\Sigma_k^2,
\qquad
k\in\{-1,0,+1\}.$ The time coordinate is the proper time of comoving observers. Homogeneity permits $a$ to depend on time but not position, while isotropy forbids a preferred spatial direction.

p.src:
Using a radial coordinate $r$ and the unit two-sphere metric $d\Omega_2^2$, the three normalized spatial metrics are $\begin{aligned}
d\Sigma_0^2 &= dr^2+r^2d\Omega_2^2,
&& k=0,
\\
d\Sigma_{+1}^2 &= dr^2+\sin^2 r\,d\Omega_2^2,
&& k=+1,
\\
d\Sigma_{-1}^2 &= dr^2+\sinh^2 r\,d\Omega_2^2,
&& k=-1.
\end{aligned}$ At a fixed time, space is therefore flat, positively curved, or negatively curved. Multiplication by $a(t)^2$ changes every spatial distance by the same factor while preserving the normalized shape.

p.src:
Take two galaxies at fixed comoving separation $\Delta\chi$. Their physical distance is $D(t)=a(t)\Delta\chi.$ Differentiating and eliminating $\Delta\chi$ gives $\dot D=\dot a\,\Delta\chi
      =\frac{\dot a}{a}D
      =H(t)D,
\qquad
H(t)\equiv\frac{\dot a}{a}.$ Thus Hubble’s law follows kinematically from homogeneous scaling. The Hubble parameter can change with time, but at any fixed cosmic time it is the same everywhere.

p.src: How the Contents of the Universe Dilute

u.src: How the Contents of the Universe Dilute
en: How the Contents of the Universe Dilute

p.src: Friedmann’s equation is not closed until $\rho$ is known as a function of $a$. Geometry has supplied one equation; the material in the universe must supply the second relation.

p.src: For nonrelativistic matter, the number of particles in a comoving volume is fixed while the physical volume grows as $a^3$. Neglecting the particles’ small kinetic energies, $\rho_{\mathrm m}(a)=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm m,0}}{a^3}.$ Here the normalization $a=1$ may be assigned at any convenient reference epoch; only ratios of scale factors are directly meaningful.

p.src: Radiation loses energy in two ways. Its number density falls as the inverse volume, and every photon’s wavelength stretches in proportion to $a$, reducing its energy by another factor of $a^{-1}$. Therefore $\rho_{\mathrm r}(a)=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm r,0}}{a^4}.$ Because $a^{-4}$ grows faster toward the past than $a^{-3}$, radiation dominates sufficiently early even if matter dominates much later.

p.src: If matter and radiation were the only components, the sign of $k$ would strongly track the future: $k=+1$ permits recollapse, $k=0$ is the marginal case that expands forever while slowing, and $k=-1$ expands forever with curvature eventually important. Dark energy breaks that simple connection. A closed universe can expand forever, and spatial flatness by itself does not determine the ultimate fate.

en: Equation of State and the Continuity Law

p.src: Rather than memorize a separate dilution rule for every substance, characterize the material by an equation of state. The program has two parts. First derive $\rho(a)$ for a given relation between pressure and energy density. Then determine that relation from the microscopic physics of matter, radiation, or vacuum. The first part is enough for the present lecture.

p.src: Pressure is momentum flux. Molecules striking the wall of a box reverse their momentum and push on the wall; faster particles transfer more momentum and produce greater pressure. Energy density and pressure therefore cannot be chosen independently once the kind of material is specified. For a simple cosmological component we write $P=w\rho,$ where $w$ is dimensionless in units with $c=1$. Cold matter has negligible pressure and hence $w=0$. Radiation has $w=1/3$, with the factor $1/3$ reflecting the average over three spatial directions.

en: Pressure is momentum flux. Molecules striking the wall of a box reverse their momentum and push on the wall; faster particles transfer more momentum and produce greater pressure. Energy density and pressure therefore cannot be chosen independently once the kind of material is specified. Radiation has $w=1/3$, with the factor $1/3$ reflecting the average over three spatial directions.

p.src: Thermodynamics in a Comoving Box

u.src: Thermodynamics in a Comoving Box
en: Thermodynamics in a Comoving Box

p.src:
Take a comoving box with physical volume $V$, energy density $\rho$, and total energy $E=\rho V.$ The first law is $dE=T\,dS-P\,dV.$ Cosmological expansion is treated as adiabatic, so $dS=0$ for the comoving box and $dE=-P\,dV.$ The minus sign says that an expanding system does work and loses internal energy. Differentiating $E=\rho V$ independently gives $dE=\rho\,dV+V\,d\rho.$ Equating the two expressions, $\begin{aligned}
\rho\,dV+V\,d\rho&=-P\,dV,\\
V\,d\rho&=-(\rho+P)\,dV.
\end{aligned}$ With $P=w\rho$, $\frac{d\rho}{\rho}=-(1+w)\frac{dV}{V}.$ Integration gives $\rho\propto V^{-(1+w)}.$ Since a comoving volume scales as $V\propto a^3$, $\boxed{\rho(a)\propto a^{-3(1+w)}}.$ In differential form, the same statement is the local energy-conservation equation $\dot\rho+3H(\rho+P)=0.$ This local conservation law remains exact even though a changing cosmological geometry need not admit a globally conserved total energy.

p.src: Vacuum Energy and the Failure of the Curvature-Fate Rule

u.src: Vacuum Energy and the Failure of the Curvature-Fate Rule
en: Vacuum Energy and the Failure of the Curvature-Fate Rule

p.src:
Dark energy introduces the equation of state $P=-\rho,
\qquad
w=-1.$ Negative pressure is tension: instead of pushing outward on the wall of a box, the contents pull inward on it. A stretched spring is a familiar object with tension, though it is only an analogy and not a microscopic model of vacuum energy.

p.src: Substituting $w=-1$ into equation  gives $\rho_\Lambda\propto a^0=\text{constant}.$ As a comoving region expands, its volume and total vacuum energy increase together, leaving the energy per unit volume unchanged. The work term in equation  accounts for that behavior because $P$ is negative. Once such a component is present, positive spatial curvature no longer guarantees recollapse.

p.src: What to Carry Forward

u.src: What to Carry Forward
en: What to Carry Forward

p.src: The cosmological principle is an averaged geometrical assertion: every point and direction is equivalent after local structure is smoothed away. It restricts the spatial metric to the three constant-curvature cases and packages all time dependence into $a(t)$: $ds^2=-dt^2+a(t)^2d\Sigma_k^2.$ Comoving separations then obey $\dot D=HD$, while bound systems need not join that flow.

p.src: Einstein’s time-time equation turns the ansatz into dynamics: $H^2+\frac{k}{a^2}=\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho.$ Its resemblance to the Newtonian energy equation is real, but general relativity identifies the integration slot with intrinsic spatial curvature and allows every form of energy to contribute.

\qquad
\rho\propto a^{-3(1+w)}.$ Matter, radiation, and vacuum energy correspond respectively to $w=0,\qquad w=\frac13,\qquad w=-1.$ Their different dilution rates determine which component controls the expansion at each epoch. The next task is to understand the physics behind these equations of state and the acceleration produced by vacuum energy.
